The call ⁠on Monday came three days after the pontiff asked Putin to arrange a ceasefire so aid could enter Oleshky, a request the Kremlin did ⁠not address when it said Putin would help organise supplies.

articles.title: ‘Once-in-a-lifetime chance’: Japan launches historic mission to collect rocks from Mars’s moon Phobos
articles.summary: Scientists hope Martian material collected will shed light on the origins of the solar system and life on Earth
body: Japan has successfully launched a spacecraft on an unprecedented mission to bring back samples from one of Mars’s moons that scientists hope will shed light on the origins of the solar system and life on Earth.

The Martian ⁠Moons Exploration (MMX) spacecraft, propelled by Japan’s flagship H3 rocket, lifted off before dawn from Tanegashima island in the country’s far south-west, the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (Jaxa) said.

The spacecraft is expected to reach Mars’s orbit in August next year and collect at least 10g of soil and rock from the surface of Phobos, one of two small, potato-shaped moons orbiting the planet. It is scheduled to return in 2031, Jaxa said.
Related: Rivers of magma once bubbled beneath crust of Mars, research suggests
The pock-marked moon, which has a diameter measuring 14 miles (22.5km), orbits Mars three times a day about 6,000km above its surface.

The flagship H3 rocket carrying the unmanned probe blasted off into a pitch black sky from Tanegashima Space Centre at 4:41am, witnessed by thousands of people who had woken up early to follow a livestream.
An hour later, Jaxa scientists declared the launch a success when the spacecraft separated from the rocket’s upper stage, prompting scenes of celebration in the flight control room.

Nasa has landed nine spacecraft on Mars over the past half a century, while China landed on the Martian surface in 2021, but this is the first time anyone has attempted to land on Phobos or the planet’s smaller moon, Deimos.
“There’s a lot of adrenaline and a lot of excitement and a lot of wow,” said Nasa astrophysicist Tom Statler, who is involved in the Japan-led project to collect samples.
Five space agencies are collaborating on the five-year mission, which will attempt to land a robotic prospector and a rover on Phobos, the larger and closer of the two moons.

The $578m mission features a five-tonne spacecraft that will sync with Phobos’ tight orbit around Mars when it arrives next summer. It will then eject a small French-German rover, named Idefix after the white terrier in the Asterix comics.

If all goes according to plan, the four-wheeled rover will bounce (due to gravity on Phobos being 1/1,000th as strong as Earth) for several minutes on Mars’s surface before coming to a halt. It will spend 100 days surveying the planet’s surface to find safe landing and sampling sites ahead of the arrival of the main craft, a four-legged stationary lander that will gather the samples.

The lander will spend only two hours on Phobos drilling and vacuuming up material, before launching back into space. Officials said it would observe Deimos during several flybys before leaving Mars’s orbit in November 2030.
“It is a once-in-a-lifetime chance. We are part of the first sample return mission from the Martian system,” said the Germany Space Agency’s rover chief Markus Grebenstein.

Scientists hope the samples will help them establish how Phobos and Deimos were formed and even offer clues about the origins of life. MMX’s findings will also help shape future Mars missions, including crewed expeditions, Nasa said.

According to one theory – the “giant impact” hypothesis – the two moons formed after a celestial body collided with Mars. A second proposition, known as the “capture” hypothesis, suggests that the moons are asteroids pulled in by Mars’s gravity.

Determining which theory is correct will help reveal “how a habitable environment for life might have arisen on the terrestrial planets”, Jaxa said, referring to the four planets closest to the sun: Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars.

The US and China are in a race to be the first to return rock samples from the surface of Mars. Nasa’s Perseverance rover, which has been roaming across Mars since 2021, has already collected samples, but its return to Earth was halted by the Trump administration after a congressional vote in January this year.
China’s Tianwen-3 spacecraft is scheduled to launch around 2028 and could bring back Mars samples as early as 2031, potentially before the Japanese moon mission’s return.

articles.title: France imposes partial curfews in several cities, including parts of Paris
articles.summary: Interior minister concedes police ‘lost control’ of weekend protests as PM vows to restore public order
body: Partial curfews have been issued for a number of French cities, including parts of Paris, after the government admitted police had “lost control” during violent weekend protests around the country.

Sébastien Lecornu, the French prime minister, said after an emergency cabinet meeting on Monday he was “fully resolved to restore public order” and had called for “local and partial” curfews if needed. There was “no question” of imposing a full curfew on entire cities, he said.
His office later announced partial curfews from 8pm to 6am on Monday and Tuesday nights in four northern cities, including Lille.

Police also imposed a curfew from 11pm on Monday until 6am on Tuesday in two areas in Paris: Place de la République, where rioting took place on Saturday; and the shopping neighbourhood of Les Halles, which has been subject to looting.
A statement from police said the orders banned gatherings and demonstrations and prohibited anyone from entering or remaining in the two designated areas.

France’s second city, Marseille, earlier announced independently that it had banned all gatherings and demonstrations on Monday. French unions, meanwhile, called for a new ⁠round of strikes and rallies on 5 November.
Lecornu told reporters that if declaring a state of emergency was deemed necessary “we could do so”, but ⁠added that at this stage partial curfews seemed “more appropriate”.

Lecornu’s comments came after France’s interior minister conceded that police had “lost control” in some cities during Saturday’s protests and the president, Emmanuel Macron, demanded a full security review and “new operational methods” to end the rioting.

Laurent Nuñez said on Monday there had been a “lack of anticipation” in preparations for the protests and acknowledged that police numbers had sometimes been inadequate to deal with rioters and looters on the fringes of the demonstrations.

Nuñez said intelligence had suggested there would be 200,000 demonstrators around the country. In the event, there were more than 500,000 and peaceful protests were hijacked, morphing into one of France’s most violent days of unrest in recent years.

He said he had tendered his resignation to Macron because he felt “responsible for everything that happened”. Macron refused it, demanding instead that Nuñez “take all necessary steps to ensure transparency over planning and intelligence failures”.

The protests follow weeks of demonstrations by high school students that have been marred by sometimes violent clashes with police, rocking the country six months before a crunch presidential ⁠election and amid mounting economic pressures.
Public buildings including a town hall were attacked and set ablaze and an estimated 2,000 shops were ransacked and looted, authorities have said.

France’s digital minister, Anne Le Henanff, urged online resale platforms to remove listings for “stolen items” and summoned representatives of companies including Vinted and eBay. According to the commerce ministry, representatives of Amazon, Leboncoin, Meta and TikTok were also invited.

Nuñez said 60,000 police and other security forces had been deployed around the country, but acknowledged it had not been enough to control determined, organised groups of violent rioters in major cities including Paris, Marseille and Lyon.

“You couldn’t look shopkeepers in the eye after hundreds of shops had been looted and say we hadn’t lost control,” the minister told French radio, but added that the responsibility of “rioters, looters and ultra-left militants” should not be glossed over.

The justice minister, Gérald Darmanin, also said intelligence failings had left the state vulnerable. “There’s no good policing without good intelligence,” he said, adding that many of those arrested had police records and “about 80%” were being prosecuted.
Darmanin said 2,513 people had been arrested and 67 imprisoned since the violence broke out over the weekend, Libération reported.
Some 70% of those arrested were adults and almost 1,000 police and gendarmes have been injured.

Macron’s office said in a statement on Monday that besides reviewing the security shortcomings, Nuñez had been tasked with “promptly implementing new operational methods for security forces to use on the ground in combating rioters”.

Rioting and looting continued on Sunday. The mayor of Paris, Emmanuel Grégoire, said on Monday that about 30 shops had been targeted in the capital the previous day, with a further 350 people arrested overnight.

“Maintaining public order is the responsibility of the state. It is the state that was at fault this weekend,” Grégoire said. “We have a social movement that is spreading, and no political prospect for a constructive way out. So the protests will continue.”

Marseille’s mayor, Benoît Payan, said not just democracy but “the very foundations of the Republic” had been undermined. Describing the situation as “almost insurrectional”, he said the government’s stance amounted to “petty political manoeuvring”.

On Monday, protesters blocked entrances to the Louvre Museum in support of the nationwide high school student protest movement and to denounce “police repression”. The museum could not open as scheduled because of the protest.
A leaflet displayed outside the museum read: “We are proud to announce that we are blocking the world’s largest museum.”

In a televised address on Sunday, Macron criticised the “unbridled” violence and said local authorities would be able to ban some demonstrations in the coming days, but stopped short of drastic measures such as declaring a state of emergency or curfew.

Saturday’s protests, by students, teachers, parents, unions and workers, focused on the high cost of living, an issue that also prompted demonstrations in several other European countries including Italy, Belgium and Albania over the weekend.

articles.title: Israeli police detain 10 people in rare raid against West Bank settlers
articles.summary: Move comes after US photojournalist and group of European diplomats and Palestinians were assaulted in separate attacks
body: Israeli police have detained 10 people in a rare raid against settlers, after a weekend of extreme violence in the occupied West Bank including an attack on US photojournalist Heidi Levine, which she described as an “attempted lynching”.

She was knocked down, kicked and beaten by a group of masked Israeli men as she covered the olive harvest in a Palestinian village on Friday. The militants broke four vertebrae and a rip, ripped open her finger so it required surgery and left her with lacerations across her body.
“I was practically, basically lynched by a gang of Jewish settlers in the area of Ramallah,” Levine said, in an interview with the BBC from her hospital bed on Monday.

The day after that assault, Israeli militants armed with sticks and iron bars attacked a group of European diplomats and Palestinians harvesting olives outside the town of Taybeh, assaulting a visiting French mayor, smashing the window of an official car, and causing severe injuries to a young Palestinian man.
The Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, questioned the accounts of Israeli militant violence, ignoring extensive video and witness evidence.
He referenced an “alleged attack” on Levine, whose severe injuries were visible in interviews from her hospital bed, and “unproven allegations” the diplomats had been targeted by militants.

The attacks and his response drew a furious international reaction, including from the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, the US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee – generally considered a staunch ally of the current Israeli government – European nations and the editor of the Washington Post, Matt Murray.
On Monday morning Israeli police released footage of a rare raid on settlers, and said they had detained 10 people connected with the attacks on foreigners and construction of an illegal outpost.
Hours later a court extended the detention of six men connected with the attacks on foreigners, to between three and four days.
There has been little response to extreme violence against Palestinians across the West Bank, and Levine said the global focus on her attack highlighted extreme double standards.
“People are dealing with this, undergoing attacks, losing property, losing family members, being injured all across the West Bank and nothing is being done,” she said.
Israelis target Palestinians with near total impunity in the occupied West Bank, where arrests are unusual, indictments rare and convictions even more unusual.

Israeli human rights group Yesh Din has documented 561 incidents of settler and soldier violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank over three weeks since 27 September. That is an average of more than 26 each day.

“It is telling that it took attacks on foreign nationals to prompt a significant response from Israeli authorities,” said the group’s executive director, Ziv Stahl. “Palestinians have endured years of systematic settler violence, with 94% of investigations into cases of settler violence against Palestinians closed without indictments.

Levine said her body armour and helmet had prevented even more serious injuries, and she considered herself “lucky” given the ferocity of the attack. Netanyahu’s attempt to cast doubt on the attack felt like a “a big slap on my face”, she added.

Netanyahu’s statements, apparently undermined by security forces arrests days later, were widely seen as an attempt to court far-right voters inside Israel, as the country heads into the final days of an election campaign.

His coalition partners include extremist settlers, who support the campaign of violence that has driven thousands of Palestinians from their homes and land in the occupied West Bank over the last three years.

Haaretz reported on Monday that political pressure was preventing the army from confronting “Jewish terrorism” in the West Bank, even when the targets were foreigners including diplomats and journalists.
Commanders are reluctant to challenge settler leaders, or take action against Israeli civilians and soldiers who attack Palestinians, Israeli defence officials told the paper.
Formal investigations and disciplinary procedures are limited and undermined by unofficial but clear messages of support from top commanders, the report said.

It cited the response to an attack on a CNN crew in March. Central Command chief Maj Gen Avi Bluth suspended the battalion responsible from operational duty and announced disciplinary action against soldiers involved.
Later that night, the brigade commander came to a base where the soldiers were staying to express his support and join them in prayer, Haaretz said.

articles.title: Houthi attack kills 53 in biggest single loss of life since Yemen civil war reignited
articles.summary: More than 200 mostly young people said to be injured after ballistic missile attack on training camp for government forces
body: At least 53 people have been killed in a Houthi ballistic missile attack on a training camp for Yemeni government security forces, making it the largest single loss of life since the country’s civil war reignited in September.

The attack on al-Alam camp in the southern Shabwa province was said to have injured more than 200 others, mostly young recruits, and was described as a disaster by the country’s UN-recognised government. The injured were taken from the police and army training camp in the Jardan district to a hospital in the local capital, Ataq, where pleas for blood donations were made.
Related: Yemen civil war: what sparked latest escalation and who is involved?

There will be an inquiry into how so many troops were left so exposed to a Houthi attack. In mid-September, the group began a fresh push on forces backing the UN-recognised government by pushing south along the Red Sea coast to try to take control of the Bab al-Mandab waterway.

Reliable assessments of the death toll in the fighting over the last month are hard to gather, but it is running into the many thousands. A Saudi airstrike on Sunday killed nine, including five children and two women.

Rashad al-Alimi, the president of the UN-recognised government, said those killed on Monday were new recruits, and he vowed an immediate hard response. He said the incident “affirmed that targeting the recruits reflects the Houthi militias’ approach of resorting to cowardly terrorist attacks whenever they face pressures or their Iranian-backed sabotage plots falter”.
On Monday he phoned the UN secretary general, António Guterres, to ask for the UN to classify the Houthis as a foreign terrorist organisation.

The Shabwa provincial authority said: “Targeting recruits constitutes a military escalation and a blatant assault on the province’s security.” Its governor, Awad bin al-Wazir, visited the wounded in hospitals, and called for extra air defences, saying troops were fighting across six fronts.

The killings underline the dangers of large numbers of troops gathering in one place within reach of the Houthi ballistic missile arsenal. The training camp was struck by three ballistic missiles while the recruits lined up in formation.
Houthi forces have also cut the road between government-run Shabwa and the Houthi-run Bayda governorate.

The Houthi military spokesperson said: “Our armed forces targeted the Saudi enemy’s mobilisations in al-Alam camp, which is run by Saudi officers in the eastern regions. The targeting resulted in the fall of dozens of dead and wounded from the Saudi enemy’s mobilisations, including Saudi officers.

“We warn the deceived ones against responding to the Saudi enemy’s calls to lure them with his defiled money to the pyres of death, and to exploit them instead of his soldiers who are indifferent to their lives.”

A Yemen government spokesperson said the site struck was not a military target linked to the current fighting but “a training centre where new recruits in the internal security forces of Shabwa governorate receive training and qualification programmes.”
They added: “This reveals the criminal nature of this assault, which targeted young people in the preparation and qualification phase to carry out their security duties, far from the frontlines.”

Separately the Houthis claim to have hit the anti-Houthi Giant Brigades of southern Yemen in six strikes in the areas of al-Suqya and Ras al-Ara. Southern forces are said to have been making progress in edging Houthi forces out of control of the area around the Bab al-Mandab strait, the narrowest waterway taking ships from the Red Sea to the Indian Ocean.

Fighting is also under way as Houthis try to mount a siege of Taiz, where citizens have been calling for greater air protection. In the city there seems to be a determination not to capitulate, but conditions are deteriorating as Houthis close access points.
It is not clear whether the Houthis have decided to slow the pace of attacks on Saudi airports and energy installations, or they are running low on munitions.
The Saudi Aramco headquarters was struck last weekend and some airlines have said they will not yet resume using Riyadh airport. The airport reopened at the weekend after being attacked this month.

Egypt’s parliament has postponed a vote on whether to send troops to Saudi Arabia despite extending the debate to a second day as MPs demanded more than two minutes each to speak. The vote is now likely to be held next week.

A two-thirds majority is required, and some opposition parties have signalled their intention to vote against or abstain. Disputes centre on the extent of the mission and whether it will involve sending troops into Yemen to help Saudi Arabia, and whether Egyptian troops inside Saudi Arabia would become targets for Houthi attacks.
The delay also gives the Egyptians time to see if Iran can persuade the Houthis to hold back, and for Saudi Arabia to confirm the renewal of badly needed loans to Egypt.

Egypt has resisted any ground intervention in Yemen, dating back to the 1962-67 war, when Gamal Abdel Nasser sent troops to back the republicans in North Yemen against the Saudi- and British-backed royalists. The incursion was intended to be minimal, but escalated to as many as 70,000 soldiers. Estimates of Egyptians killed range from 10,000-26,000.

articles.title: Why are people protesting across Europe?
articles.summary: School conditions, unaffordable housing and the cost of living have brought demonstrators on to the streets in several countries
body: Young people have been taking to the streets across Europe, including in Spain, France and Portugal, to protest over their unhappiness at the state of schools and the wider cost of living crisis.

In France, high school pupils have clashed with police in often violent protests over long hours, missing teachers, dilapidated classrooms and an opaque university admissions system. Pupils routinely miss months of teaching due to unfilled staff absences.

Other demonstrators soon joined in, voicing their unhappiness about rising living costs, including over fuel prices after US bombing in effect caused the closure of the strait of Hormuz. The General Confederation of Labour, one of France’s largest unions, has backed the protests and called for lower prices, higher pensions and boosted wages.
The French president, Emmanuel Macron, is nearing the end of his time in the Élysée Palace after serving two terms.
Over the Pyrenees in Spain, activists took to the streets in September over housing prices.

The protests were triggered by the eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her home after an investment fund hiked her rent by 230%. Maricarmen Abascal died a fortnight later after being admitted to hospital.
Protesters have called for rent freezes, halting the evictions of vulnerable people and the regulation of short-term and room rentals.

Similar pleas were made across the Iberian border in Portugal on Saturday, when hundreds gathered in central Lisbon. Portuguese housing prices more than doubled between 2015 and 2024, roughly twice as fast as the EU average, according to official data.

Squeezed household budgets were also at the centre of marches in Milan. Masked rioters seemingly later seized on the protests to throw stones, paving blocks and other objects at riot police and setting fire to barricades made from bar tables. There were also clashes between police and protesters in Turin and Bologna.

Meanwhile, protests in Albania against the prime minister, Edi Rama, entered their seventh day on Monday. Demonstrators have said they are unhappy with perceived corruption, a lack of jobs and poor education standards.
The education protests in France began in late September, a week after the start of the school year. Protests soon also began springing up in Portugal and Belgium.

In France, demonstrations reached a high point on Saturday as about half a million people turned out to protest against the surging cost of living and join the students demanding better conditions at their schools. That day there were also marches in Belgium, Portugal and Italy.
In Albania, protests have been taking place since the summer, triggered by a luxury coastal development backed by Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner.

In France, the government has said it will deploy 3,000 more substitute teachers to deal with shortages, and include students in decision-making for schools. It also scrapped plans to increase some university registration fees, which it had announced for next year’s budget.
Fuel protests in mid-September led to an announcement by the Élysée that the government would increase petrol subsidies for certain industries.

Spain’s Socialist prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, attempted to pass emergency housing legislation that included a ban on evictions until 2030 and the regulation of temporary lettings and lettings by room.

The legislation’s defeat at the hands of rightwing and far-right parties in parliament led Sánchez to call a snap election for 29 November, as he told the public he needed a “broader progressive majority” to get new reforms through.

In recent days, the protests have been eclipsed by the violence that played out on the fringes. On Sunday night Macron said it was “unbearable to see our streets ransacked” while, hours later, France’s prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, called for “very limited” and “localised” curfews.

Macron said a distinction must be drawn between what he described as genuine, peaceful demonstrators who were making demands over the cost of living and the education system, and others who “destroy, ransack and loot”.

His interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, appeared to signal the French government was not willing to concede further, as he blamed “far-left” protesters and “criminals who looted and ransacked” buildings across France. The country will go to the polls in April 2027.
Meanwhile, the protests continue. In Paris, about a dozen demonstrators blocked the entrance to the Louvre on Monday, leaving tourists milling outside the world’s most-visited museum.
In Spain, housing campaigners have vowed to keep up the pressure on politicians to address soaring costs, announcing plans for a general strike on 11 November.

articles.title: Ferocious criticism from all sides underlines Macron’s isolation
articles.summary: French president has compounded impression of arrogance with strategic errors – and consequences could be profound
body: The near-universal chorus of condemnation that greeted Emmanuel Macron’s address to the nation on Sunday, after one of the most violent days of rioting and looting in France’s recent history, was a stark reflection of just how weakened he now is.

Speaking from his office at the Élysée Palace, the president delivered an eight-minute speech expressing “anger and shame” after a weekend in which a town hall was set ablaze, 2,000-plus shops were looted, 2,300 people were arrested and 1,000 police injured.

A month-long protest by high school pupils over crumbling and crowded classrooms converged with broader frustrations over soaring living costs, rapidly widening inequality and falling public spending, bringing together students, teachers, trade unionists and a resurrected gilets jaunes movement.
Related: French prime minister calls for ‘local and partial’ curfews after riots

Those largely peaceful protests were swiftly hijacked by masked groups who torched vehicles, ransacked businesses and severely damaged public infrastructure, including setting fire to Limoges’ city hall and invading that of Marseille.

Macron acknowledged the “deep anxiety” of young people but offered no concrete policy initiatives, no cabinet reshuffle and no new public spending, merely telling his prime minister to organise consultations and asking opposition politicians to take a stand.

The response, across the political spectrum, was damning. The Greens’ leader, Marine Tondelier, said that rather than “even beginning to make any kind of mea culpa”, Macron was “summoning us to the PM’s office like pupils to the blackboard”.

On the far right, the National Rally’s Jordan Bardella called the speech “lamentable” and said Macron had “nothing left to say” to the French. The party’s figurehead, Marine Le Pen, said the country was “caught in a vice between violence and impotence”.

The centre-right’s Bruno Retailleau said Macron was “totally overwhelmed”, while on the radical left, Jean-Luc Mélenchon accused the president of relying on “inaction and police brutality” in doomed hopes that the protests would simply fizzle out.

Perhaps most damagingly, even Macron’s former prime minister Édouard Philippe said he would have preferred “decisions and initiatives that might lead to a return to order and the restoration of state authority … Our country needs to be governed.”

Criticism is to be expected from rivals positioning themselves six months before a presidential election to choose Macron’s successor. But its sheer ferocity underlines his isolation, the disdain in which he is held, and the anger he inspires.

It is a structural trap that he has largely set for himself. Macron came to power in 2017 as a “Jupiterian” president – a deliberate strategy aimed at elevating the head of state above daily politics, projecting distant authority and technocratic brilliance.

But over nine years in the Élysée, that high-handed style – partly born, his critics say, of Macron’s complete lack of basic political experience as an elected official in a town hall or as a constituency MP – has morphed into perceived arrogance and detachment.

It has been compounded by catastrophic strategic errors, and France’s spiralling economic problems. Macron lost a functional parliamentary majority by refusing to meaningfully campaign between the presidential and legislative elections of 2022.

Two years later he dissolved the national assembly. That gamble backfired spectacularly, with voters returning an even more deadlocked parliament split between a divided left, a much-diminished centrist bloc and Le Pen’s far right.

Without a working majority, the government repeatedly resorted to controversial constitutional manoeuvres to force through laws without a parliamentary vote, laying it – and Macron – open to further accusations of democratic illegitimacy.

Compounding that institutional deadlock is a looming fiscal crisis. In decades gone by, French presidents facing mass protests on the streets could in effect buy a degree of social tranquility with targeted spending packages or public sector concessions.

But France’s national debt, at 119% of GDP, is at its highest level since 1946. Its budget deficit, at 5.1%, is also among the highest in the EU. There is just no money in the bank to ease the cost of living squeeze that brought 550,000 people on to the streets on Saturday.

The markets are worried: France’s borrowing costs are higher than Greece’s. And with few fiscal options, the government’s clearest response – in time-honoured French tradition – has been teargas and baton charges, sometimes against schoolchildren, further aggravating tensions.

The consequences for the presidential election could be profound. The centrist coalition built around Macron’s brand has all but collapsed. If the protests and violence persist, the main beneficiary will be the law-and-order champions of the far right.

Jean-Baptiste Moreau, an influential former MP from Macron’s party with whom the largely lame-duck president still occasionally speaks, reportedly went so far this weekend as to suggest he should resign and call early presidential elections.
“Macron still thinks he can change things,” he told Le Monde. “But at the moment, Marine Le Pen is on a direct path to the Élysée Palace.”

articles.title: Jim Churm obituary
articles.summary: Other lives: Nurse and physiotherapist who played his part in the D-day landings as a medic on landing craft
body: My father, Jim Churm, who has died aged 102, was a D-day veteran and former Royal Navy medic; he later enjoyed a long career in nursing and physiotherapy.

Jim joined the navy as an 18-year-old during the second world war and trained as a sick berth attendant before being assigned to landing craft operations. On D-day, 6 June 1944, he sailed from Newhaven in East Sussex as the leading medic aboard a landing craft involved in the assault on Sword Beach, one of the five main landing areas along the Normandy coast during the allied invasion of France.

His primary responsibility was to care for sick and injured personnel, but with crews stretched to their limits, he also helped operate winches and undertook general seamanship duties. He had to be ready to transfer between vessels whenever medical assistance was needed.

Jim made two crossings from Britain to Normandy on landing craft that were particularly vulnerable to enemy mines, lacking the protective equipment fitted to larger naval vessels. Afterwards he spent a short time back in the UK before being posted to Egypt.

After the war he qualified as a nurse, specialising in orthopaedics in Birmingham before undertaking physiotherapy training in Liverpool and then becoming a chartered physiotherapist, first in Leicester and then in Blackburn at the Queen’s Park hospital and Blackburn Royal Infirmary.

Later he took on private work at Our Lady of Compassion hospital in the town and had his own surgeries in Accrington and Blackburn. For a time, in the late 1960s, he was also the physiotherapist for two local football clubs, Blackburn Rovers and Accrington Stanley.

Born in Nottingham, he was the son of Arthur, an oil industry worker, and his wife, Miriam (nee Cooper), who divorced when Jim was young. After attending Claremont school in Nottingham he joined the navy despite having secured an apprenticeship with a butcher, which was a reserved wartime occupation.

In later life Jim was quietly proud of the small part he played in the liberation of France, and was keen to emphasise the often-overlooked role of landing craft crews, without whom the troops could not have reached the beaches. He was a committed supporter of remembrance activities and regularly attended Royal British Legion Scotland events, where his experiences, wisdom and humility were greatly valued.

In retirement he and his wife, Sheila (nee Cahill), who was also a physiotherapist and whom he married in 1952, retired to Crossmichael in Kirkcudbrightshire, where they made their home for more than 30 years. Jim became a much-loved member of the local community and particularly enjoyed fishing on Loch Ken.

His 100th birthday was celebrated with a surprise performance by the Royal Marines Band, Scotland, and in 2025 he was made a chevalier of the Légion d’honneur by the French ambassador at the Usher Hall in Edinburgh, during a concert commemorating the 80th anniversary of VE Day.
His life, however, was defined as much by his devotion to family, and by his kindness and commitment to helping others as by his wartime experiences.
Sheila died in 2018; Jim is survived by their three sons, David, Michael and me, 10 grandchildren and five great-grandchildren.

articles.title: France hit by debt sell-off as violent protests unnerve investors
articles.summary: Difference between French and German borrowing costs widens after public buildings burned and shops looted
body: France has been hit by a fresh wave of selling in its bond and stock markets after violent protests over the weekend led to thousands of arrests and left public buildings burned and hundreds of shops looted across the country.
The chaos has spooked investors as analysts worried that it would undermine Paris’s efforts to cut spending and reduce its debt.

The yield on the government’s 10-year bonds rose by as much as 16 basis points to 4.94% on Monday. Yields rise when prices fall, and the bond market sell-off pushed France’s borrowing costs close to a 24-year high.
This widened the difference between the French and German 10-year borrowing costs – which is a metric for the risk premium attached to French debt – towards its highest level in 14 years.

Analysts at Goldman Sachs said European sovereign risk was back in focus, with fiscal concerns about France raising the question of whether there could be a repeat of the eurozone debt crisis of 15 years ago.

“The risks of disorderly market escalation and real economy contagion look notably lower. But the fundamental fiscal challenges for some countries – especially in France – look harder now than in 2011-15,” the investment bank said.
“The issue of how to deal with fundamental sovereign risk remains unresolved in the euro area, requiring credible fiscal consolidation.”
The two-year French bond yield rose by nine basis points to 3.64%.
Concerns about France’s instability knocked the euro down to a 17-month low against the pound on Monday morning, when sterling rose to €1.188.

Violence erupted across France after weeks of relatively peaceful demonstrations over conditions in schools and the cost of living, prompting the French president, Emmanuel Macron, to condemn the “unbridled violence” in a televised address on Sunday night.

Tens of thousands of people have attended peaceful marches to demand more teachers and repairs to decrepit schools, but different groups have clashed with police in cities including Paris, Bordeaux, Nice and Marseille.
Jim Reid of Deutsche Bank said the protests “won’t make it easy for the international community to be totally comfortable buying OATs”, referring to French government bonds.
“With France already facing a difficult fiscal backdrop and the 2027 election approaching, the weekend adds another layer of political risk for markets,” he said.
The 30-year bond, which is a benchmark for the French government’s long-term cost of borrowing, rose by ten basis points to 5.46%.
The rises will put further strain on France’s public finances as the government tries to pass a budget for next year to rein in its deficit.
France’s debt-to-GDP stood at 115.6% in 2025, while its budget deficit was 5.1%, compared with 94.3% and 4.3% respectively for the UK.
The unrest adds to “concerns about the political and fiscal troubles in France”, said Neil Wilson, Saxo UK’s investor strategist.
“It underscores how hard it will be for a government to enact the kind of spending restraint required to get the deficit down.”

The French government is preparing a budget that would involve cutting pensions spending and funding for government departments, excluding defence. There are growing fears, however, that political pressure could derail the plans, which could push up borrowing further and add more to the country’s debt pile.
The euro also slipped against the US dollar, down by 0.4% at one stage on Monday to $1.1197.
France’s Cac 40 index, which tracks the biggest companies listed in Paris, fell by 1.4% , compared with a 1.1% drop on the pan-European Stoxx 600 index.
French bank stocks were among the fallers, with Société Générale and BNP Paribas down more than 3%.
Other European stock markets also weakened, with Italy’s FTSE Mib down 1.6% and Spain’s Ibex dropping by 1.9%.

Daniela Hathorn, a senior market analyst at Capital.com, said investors were concerned that higher borrowing costs would increase France’s debt-servicing expenses, reducing its fiscal flexibility at a time when growth is already subdued.

“But France is not alone,” he said. “Spain faces its own political constraints around budgets and fiscal reforms, although stronger economic growth provides some protection, while Italy’s substantial debt stock leaves it particularly sensitive to prolonged periods of elevated yields.”

articles.title: People scour strait of Hormuz for spilt cargo after Iran attacks container ships
articles.summary: At least 15 vessels struck in waterway in past 10 days, with rumours that they were carrying valuable goods
body: People have been scouring the strait of Hormuz for spilt cargo after Iran attacked at least 15 container ships passing through the crucial waterway in the past 10 days.
Some ships have been hit by drones, others by mines. On Sunday, a ship was struck by a rocket-propelled grenade launched from a small boat 75 miles (120km) north-east of the Saudi port of Jubail.

The rise in Iranian attacks appears to have helped resolidify Tehran’s disputed control over the strait, as well as pushing the price of a barrel of Brent crude oil close to $108 a barrel on Monday morning.

Last Wednesday a ship travelling from Karachi, Pakistan, to Fujairah, in the United Arab Emirates, sunk after hitting a mine, according to Iranian state TV. All 21 crew members were evacuated and no injuries were reported. Dozens of its 2,500 containers were seen floating in the water. Rumours that iPhones and other expensive goods were among its cargo – fuelled by fake AI-generated photos published on social media – prompted fishers and others to investigate.
One fisher told an Iranian reporter: “The Arab boatmen, who were closer to the ship, arrived earlier than the Iranians. They used stonecutters to cut the container and took whatever was there.”

Col Javad Mokhtar Rezaei, the deputy head of cultural and social affairs for Iran’s cyber police (Fata), told the Tasnim news agency: “In some cases, the phones offered may actually exist, but exposing electronic components to salt water and extreme humidity can cause corrosion of internal components, damage to the boards, battery and display, and cause hidden malfunctions in the device’s performance.”
Meysam Doost-Mohammadi, a spokesperson for the Iranian mobile phone Aassociation, said it would be unusual for valuable devices to be transported by ship.

The bulk of the recent attacks have occurred close to the coast with Oman, a route that Iran regards as unauthorised. In the seven days to Friday 16 October, 12 vessels were attacked, according to the UK Maritime Trade Operations Centre (UKMTO).

The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) says it has the right to attack any ship that seeks to traverse the strait without its permission or with its transponders off. Officials have also ordered local fishers not to pillage the sea for luxury items, saying the goods are the property of the state.

Two oil tankers were hit on Saturday, including a supertanker carrying 2m barrels of oil, according to the IRGC. The Fars news agency published a video that appears to show the tanker burning, but which cannot be independently verified. A third tanker was hit late on Sunday.

It is disputed how many ships have been hit by mines or IRGC shelling. UKMTO’s weekly overview recorded 254 transits of the strait (125 outbound, 129 inbound) in the week to 14 October, approximately 70% below pre-conflict levels.

Dr Devaraj Asir Ramesh, of Anna University in Chennai, India, warned that the region’s marine habitats faced threats from toxic debris and oil spills, while noise might have disturbed marine life. Iranian strikes on the Emirates, he said, were likely to have contaminated seagrass beds with hydrocarbons and caused auditory damage to cetaceans – marine mammals such as dolphins and porpoises – which are sensitive to loud noise that travels through the sea.

Oil released by attacks on tankers at Fujairah could have caused ecological harm, he added. “Oil spills, chemical leaks and acoustic disturbances have impaired biodiversity, fisheries, aquaculture, desalination, and eco-tourism,” he wrote in the International Journal of Research and Innovation in Social Sciences.
On Friday, the Iranian president said the conflicts in Gaza and the wider Middle East had inflicted a significant toll on nature that extended beyond borders and required “international solutions”.

“What has occurred in our region as a result of wars of aggression is ecocide, or environmental genocide, and it must be condemned,” Masoud Pezeshkian said. He argued that countries subjected to economic sanctions or military aggression should not be forced to shoulder the financial burden of environmental damage resulting from conflicts they did not initiate.
Successive studies, mainly by US universities using satellite imagery, have warned of the dangers facing the strait.

Meanwhile, the Russian foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov, visited Tehran offering to act as an intermediary between Iran and Donald Trump, especially over the issue of Iran’s nuclear stockpile, which the US president insists must be addressed before he lifts his threat to attack Iran again.
Iran has offered to open the strait in six days in return for sanctions relief.

Russia has offered to take Iran’s stockpile of highly enriched uranium, but Iran is reluctant to make a commitment on its nuclear programme and has not given the International Atomic Energy Agency access to its bombed nuclear sites since June 2025. Lavrov also proposed a trilateral summit between China, Russia and Iran to agree new security architecture for the strait. He said the region was on the verge of a full-scale crisis.

Tehran is braced for another attack soon, especially after the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, launched a new national security doctrine on Sunday that included an emphasis on prevention and offence, including pre-emptive strikes on potential threats.

articles.title: Ebola cases in Kenya highlight US failures amid Trump cuts to key services
articles.summary: Opposition to US-led quarantine center in Kenya follows sweeping funding cuts and withdrawal from WHO
body: An eighth person in Kenya has tested positive for the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola in the country’s first-ever cluster of cases of the virus, as the second-largest outbreak in history has killed more than 4,300 and sickened more than 9,000 people in the region.

It highlights the diminished role the US has played in the worsening Ebola outbreak by building a controversial quarantine center in Kenya, pulling back health support globally, and banning travelers from certain countries. All of this has also reduced the ability to identify and respond to the outbreak and exacerbated mistrust.

The US created a controversial quarantine center at Kenya’s Laikipia airbase, where Americans returning from the Democratic Republic of the Congo would be required to quarantine. The center, opposed by locals, has stirred distrust in the Kenyan government, leading to protests and a Kenyan court ordering a halt to the center.

“Many Kenyans were concerned about the fact that there was no information and people did not know why the quarantine place was being set up, who was actually going to use it, and what had informed that,” said Allan Maleche, executive director of the Kenya Legal & Ethical Issues Network on HIV and Aids (Kelin). The litigation will be decided in November, he said.
In the meantime, Kenyans were “very cautious around any information that is being given by the government around Ebola”, Maleche said.

Americans who questioned whether the US has the legal authority to quarantine Americans on foreign soil and prevent them from returning home are pushing back against the quarantine center as Kenya faces its first Ebola cases.

“Is this still a viable solution for the US?” asked Jennifer Nuzzo, director of the pandemic center at Brown University school of public health. “Are we posing not only an undue burden on the Kenyan government to be able to handle this, but also is this the safest place to be bringing Americans?”
The US already has “world-class” Ebola treatment units, Nuzzo pointed out.

“American taxpayers built these units for precisely this purpose, and it’s mind-boggling to me that we’re going to leave them empty,” she said. In previous outbreaks, actively ill patients have been evacuated safely to these centers, where they have recovered without further spread of the virus.

The unease follows sweeping cuts to US health support across the world, with the demolition of the US Agency for International Development (USAID) and cuts to funding and staff at health agencies like the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

On 1 October, the CDC closed HIV prevention offices in Angola and South Sudan, with plans to close offices in Zimbabwe. The US has slashed programs across the world – including DR Congo, where the Ebola outbreak is centered, and other countries, like Kenya, bracing for cases as the outbreak widens.
“We have had a lot of concerns after the US first cut funding for HIV promptly without any direction,” Maleche said. “It led to clinics closing. It led to a lot of anxiety among people.”

The US is now negotiating bilateral agreements with each country, including Kenya – a process that has been mired in secrecy, Maleche said. “It’s not very clear what’s the plan, who’s rolling it out, and what will be involved.”

Cuts to decades-long programs mean the affected countries and the US have less insight into what’s happening, in addition to a lessened ability to prevent and stop outbreaks. “When you pull back on those, not only do you leave those countries less prepared to deal with that day-to-day threat, but it also means that they’re less prepared to deal with future emergencies,” Nuzzo said.

The US officially left the World Health Organization (WHO) in January, making it much harder to collaborate on the response to crises like these. When the US left the WHO, it also “pulled out a substantial amount of funding”, said Maleche. That means the WHO’s response had also been “weakened”, he said.

A Kenyan man fell ill in DRC before traveling by road to Uganda and then flying to Nairobi on 3 October, where he died in a hospital two days later. Since then, seven close contacts have tested positive.
Patrick Amoth, the director-general for health, confirmed on Sunday the total number of ‌infections in the country was eight.
Kenya’s ministry of health pointed to the success of contact tracing and quarantine. About 108 people have been quarantined in Nairobi.

“The general feeling is that the contact tracing systems are working,” Maleche said. But Kenyans are also wondering why there were “many lapses” that resulted in a sick person traveling across countries. The border between DR Congo and Uganda has been closed since May. Uganda was declared Ebola-free in August after earlier reporting 20 cases and two deaths.
A French doctor who returned from DR Congo in June tested positive, and several Americans have been evacuated from DR Congo to Europe for Ebola treatment or monitoring.

In Kenya, “the biggest fear is around how will other countries react” to the outbreak, with travel bans a particular worry, Maleche said. The US put travel bans in place from DR Congo and neighboring Uganda and South Sudan once the outbreak was detected in May, but it would be “very ironic” if the US instituted travel bans, given its quarantine center in Kenya, Maleche said.

Raphael Warnock, a Democratic senator from Georgia, and Bill Cassidy, a Republican senator from Louisiana, penned a letter in June to the Senate appropriations committee opposing the Trump administration’s plans to cut back on HIV prevention and monitoring.

Dismantling of USAID, withdrawing from the WHO, and abruptly cutting foreign aid cuts was “degrading our outbreak preparedness” and had “seriously weakened our ability to keep Americans safe from infectious disease”, Warnock said in a statement.

“These cuts to global health funding have led to the erosion of international disease-monitoring infrastructure that helps us catch threats like Ebola before they reach our shores, at a time when the world needs American leadership most.” The US should be strengthening these systems, not abandoning them, he said.

Nuzzo agreed. “It’s about having an understanding of the systems and the conditions in other countries, and eyes and ears in those countries to detect when something out of the ordinary happens, and to get that information as early as possible,” she said. That benefits the US and the countries themselves, she said.

Work such as HIV prevention “can be repurposed”, she added. “You have connections with clinical care, the ability to move medicines, the ability to conduct laboratory tests, the ability to move specimens around – all of those capacities are things that you would use in other disease emergencies.”

articles.title: Albania accused of rushing through Trump-linked resort in formerly protected landscape
articles.summary: Dutch MEP says government is trying to avoid EU environmental rules as protests over luxury development turn violent
body: MEPs have accused Albania of deploying “sneaky” practices to fast-track a proposed Trump-linked luxury resort in the country amid protests that have turned increasingly violent.

As the prime minister, Edi Rama, pledged to “listen to the voices of young people” taking to the streets, there was mounting criticism of his failure to address demonstrators who had long opposed the controversial project peacefully.

In scenes not seen in decades, students now leading the unrest have fought pitched battles with riot police in Tirana as ministerial buildings, banks and businesses have been set ablaze, attacked and looted.
Speaking to the Guardian, the Dutch MEP Tineke Strik accused Rama of inflaming the situation by doggedly pursuing plans championed by the US president’s son-in-law Jared Kushner.

“If the Albanian government had taken the ‘Flamingo Revolution’ seriously we wouldn’t be here,” she said of the popular movement launched in response to the resort being built in ecologically sensitive areas of the Balkan state. “The students are voicing the frustration of people who feel that they haven’t been listened to.”
Related: Why are people protesting across Europe?

On Monday, municipal workers could be seen removing paving stones as shopkeepers secured premises with metal sheeting following a sixth consecutive day of violent clashes in the capital in which protestors also set fire to a police station. Riot police responded with rubber bullets and tear gas as they attempted to disperse the crowds. Students have vowed to continue demonstrating until the socialist leader resigns – a demand he has resolutely refused to meet.

“This terrible resort idea was the match that lit this fire,” sighed Greta, a student in Tirana, adding that the slogan chanted by young people attending demonstrations for months had been “Albania is not for sale”.
“Now there are other issues that are whipping up the flames. We actually really care about the state of our democracy, about living standards, about education.”

The controversial project foresees construction of up to 10,000 villas in coastal areas that were environmentally protected until the government passed a contentious law allowing “strategic investors” to build in parts of the Vjosa-Narta landscape surrounding the last intact delta system in the Mediterranean.

In June, the European parliament called for the legislation to be repealed by the EU candidate country, saying it posed a direct threat to environmental standards that are “non-negotiable conditions of accession”.

The parliament’s move came after construction workers broke ground in May, igniting protests that would spread nationwide after it was discovered that ancient dunes and forest had been destroyed to create access roads in the nature reserve.

Re-elected for a historic fourth term last year, Rama is on a mission to get the Balkan state – still one of Europe’s poorest after the collapse of communism more than three decades ago – into the 27-member bloc by 2030. In a live address delivered on social media on Sunday he said: “Albanians need to think very clearly: do they want this, do they want that, or do they want the EU?”

But Strik, a Greens group MEP who led a European parliament fact-finding mission to Albania in June, said it was clear the government was also rushing to “create facts on the ground” before it was bound by EU standards. A frontrunner in the enlargement process, Albania hopes to wrap up accession talks by the end of 2027.

Citing an environmental impact study whose “scientific results” Rama recently described as key to the €4bn project going ahead, she said: “The government has submitted an environmental package to the [EU] Commission but without repealing the law allowing for construction in the protected area … it is still trying to help realise the megalomaniacal luxury resort plans of Ivanka Trump and Jared Kushner. How? By conducting a fast-track impact assessment which, if [more comprehensively] done, could never lead to the conclusion that this construction is allowed.”

Rama told a tourism forum in Brussels this month that the milestone development would be a gamechanger for a nation that had been the “North Korea” of Europe before the fall of its Stalinist regime in the 1990s.

“If construction goes ahead this will be decided not in the streets but by science,” he told the forum. “The idea that nature will take care of itself, if we simply look at it, is preposterous and old. We are trying to come out with … a [high-end] destination where nature will be highlighted and where people will holiday, and where the Albanian people will get back what they deserve: a much stronger economy.”

On 8 October, Kushner described the venture as having a single goal: “To build to the highest design and environmental standards and leave this extraordinary part of Albania greener, more biodiverse and environmentally stronger”.
Related: Albania’s prime minister vows not to resign over student-led protests

Private contractors, tasked with implementing the impact study, have been seen mapping, measuring and monitoring the area, prompting environmentalists, who had initially spearheaded the protests, to counter this week that “science had already spoken”.

“It spoke when experts from the faculty of science at Tirana University elected to protect this incredible landscape in 2004,” said Aleksander Trajce at the country’s oldest conservation group, the Protection and Preservation of the Natural Environment in Albania (PPNEA). “Their decision was based on very sound scientific data. There’s no way that science can tell us more. Reopening the discussion is not only disingenuous but clearly a way to justify construction that should not be happening at all.”

Insisting an environmental impact assessment would take “at least two years” to be properly conducted, he added: “You’d need several seasons, across several years, to really examine the species and biodiversity of the region.”

With the violence showing no sign of abating, Albanians feel very angry at the EU’s lacklustre stance, said Trajce. “If it had intervened earlier and told Rama to stop, the peaceful phase of the protest movement would not have escalated into what it is today.”

Saying she had been surprised by the Albanian prime minister’s enthusiasm for such a large-scale tourism complex in an area so fragile, Strik emphasised the importance of protecting such unique shorelines on a continent that had learned from past mistakes. “I accuse Rama of serving his own interests and the interests of Kushner and not the interests of the environment and the Albanian people,” she said.

“The government clearly intends to finalise the procedures before it is legally bound by EU standards. Such sneaky and disloyal practices should be strongly criticised by the EU. If Albania seriously wants to be a reliable candidate member state, it should respect EU law and not try to circumvent it.”

Asked about Strik’s claims, Rama told the Guardian: “Please tell the honourable lady that the violence in Tirana is very real. Instead of imagining environmental plots that do not exist, she could help Albania by condemning the violence she appears to appreciate, in an unfortunate echo of the Kremlin’s own lady, Madam Zakharova [Russian foreign ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova].”

articles.title: ‘It looks like a war zone’: France reels as looting continues for second night
articles.summary: Police appear to have been taken by surprise by scale of looting that began after protests turned violent in Paris and other cities
body: Just before 1am on Monday morning, two motorbikes carrying one passenger each stopped at a traffic light on a backstreet near rue de Rivoli, one of central Paris’s busiest shopping streets.

“You’ve got to go where there are a lot of people, where they’ve done the shop windows,” said one motorbike rider to another. Minutes later 10 other men, their faces covered with ski balaclavas, came down the street on foot pursued by a police van.

Soon after Emmanuel Macron’s televised speech on Sunday night telling the nation it was “unbearable to see our streets ransacked”, groups of men looted shops in central Paris for hours for a second night running. Dozens of people attempted to smash windows near Les Halles shopping centre and grab goods. Others broke into an electrical shop in Belleville in the north of the city.
“Men were battering shop windows, trying to break in, then they were chased by police,” said a 73-year-old woman near Les Halles.

“There were different groups running everywhere with police chasing on foot or by car, and at the same time, some people were setting bins and bikes alight. The groups breaking into shops aren’t hostile to passersby so you’d see local residents walking down the street on their way home late at night, and masked teenagers running past in the other direction carrying looted goods. It’s so strange – it’s like two different universes in parallel worlds.”

She said: “It says a lot about society – it shows we have neglected our education system and that we’re living in a consumer society where all we say to our young people is: ‘buy, buy, buy’. In this type of extreme capitalism, some people don’t have enough money to buy all of this and so they attack.”
Nearby, an optician’s shop on rue Beaubourg had had its window smashed and the whole glass front dragged out on to the pavement. Its spectacle shelves had been emptied.

The looting in Paris and other cities across France had begun on Saturday. That day, police faced three distinct groups. First, peaceful demonstrators calling for better funding for schools and public services marched calmly in cities cross France, including schoolchildren, parents, grandparents and teachers.

Separately to those peaceful protesters, other groups made barricades of burning bikes, clashed with police and targeted state buildings, such as the town hall in the central city of Limoges, in what local mayors described as unprecedented violence. Finally, looters had run around city streets smashing shop windows and taking goods.
The police appear to have been taken by surprise by a second night of looting in central Paris on Sunday night and into the early hours of Monday.

The identities of looters was not known. Some people seen looting in central Paris over the weekend appeared to be teenagers. Some had struggled to carry many shoeboxes in their arms as they ran down the street from a smashed designer trainer shop in the Marais area. But there was also a large presence of masked adult men.

The justice minister, Gérald Darmanin, on Monday said that men arrested in vandalised shops on Saturday night included a 34-year-old who had previous convictions for criminal damage, theft, violence and driving offences. Others included a 46-year-old carrying clothes from a shop, a 23-year-old drunk man allegedly carrying the keys of a stolen scooter and a 19-year-old arrested while he was hiding in the changing room of a vandalised shop, and who had previous convictions for drug-dealing.

In some parts of central Paris with no police presence on Saturday night, dozens of people had been seen running with armfuls of shoes or perfume boxes. On Sunday morning, some shopping streets in Paris woke up to smashed glass and piles of empty shoeboxes where looters had grabbed designer trainers and run, or even boxes of hair-dye. Shops that advertised buying and selling gold near Place de la République had signs and windows smashed as groups tried to break in.

The fact that looting had continued for a second night worried shopkeepers on Monday morning. Some had tried to protect their businesses. Others were emptying stock. An Adidas shop near Les Halles in central Paris was packing its contents into a large van on Monday morning to avoid theft. “Don’t worry, we’re not looters,” said the removal men to passersby as they wheeled out racks of tracksuits.

At Paris’s Place de la République police had fired teargas and charged as crowds of hundreds of people had gathered to stand in the square on Sunday afternoon. Into the night on Sunday, further up boulevard de Sébastopol, dozens of people had shouted anti-police slogans and thrown glass bottles in the direction of officers. On Monday morning, burnt bikes and scooters were piled up on street corners and the road had patches of melted asphalt.
Graffiti along the roads leading from République included “Tax the Rich” outside a bank whose windows had been smashed.

“It looks like a war zone around here,” said a one charity worker near Place de la République on Monday morning as he looked at a burnt-out cafe-bar north of the main square, which had been torched on Saturday. “There’s a general angst out there and people want to make that known, you can’t deny it. But people who are smashing and destroying things, that’s taking it too far.”

A digital special effects worker with an office nearby said: “This was the bar where we often went for a drink after work. There are looters who are taking advantage of the demonstrations to create chaos … We don’t know when this is going to end. There has always been a bit of trouble in Paris after protests, but this is on a whole different scale.”

articles.title: ‘Narcos have one language – violence’: the activist defying France’s biggest drug cartel after his brothers’ murder
articles.summary: Amine Kessaci, 23, lives under constant threat as trial of five men becomes focus of nation’s battle with mafia-style crime
body: At 23, he is one of the most heavily protected people in France, constantly sleeping in different locations to escape the threat of contract killers from the country’s biggest drug cartel.

“Narcos and drug traffickers only have one language, one method: violence,” said Amine Kessaci, a young law student from a Marseille housing estate, who, after the murders of his two brothers, has become the most outspoken voice against the Latin American-style narco gangs expanding their reach across France.

“Violence is all the [narco bosses] understand, so as soon as they have someone facing them who speaks out, who puts the reality into words, who organises solidarity with others, they see a competitor for their influence on the ground. They try to silence that voice, and that’s what they’re doing with me,” he said.

On Monday, a courtroom in the southern town of Aix-en-Provence became the focus of France’s battle with mafia-style drug dealers, who the government has said now pose a greater risk to the nation than terrorism.

The crisis of France’s Latin American-style cartels has become a key battleground before the 2027 presidential election as the right and the far right accuse the government of failing to stop drug barons who boast an annual turnover of billions of euros and who have ordered dozens of killings in recent years.

Five men with alleged connections to a major Marseille-based organised crime group, known as DZ Mafia, are on trial for the murder of Kessaci’s elder brother, Brahim, and the three-week hearing hopes to expose the reality of cartel bosses so powerful they can allegedly order killings from jail. The five men deny the charges.

Kessaci was 17 and living on a low-income housing estate in the Mediterranean port city when Brahim, 22, who had been recruited to a drug gang as a teenager, was shot and then burned in a car by a Marseille motorway in 2020.
It was a brutal killing of a style that has become a regular event in Marseille and beyond.

From the 1930s to the 1970s, Marseille was a centre for heroin processing factories, exporting the lucrative drug to the US. But in the past two decades, the drug trade of cannabis and cocaine has focused on French consumption, recruiting local children as what Kessaci calls “child soldiers” and filling an economic void in the deindustrialised city, where some northern tower blocks have high youth unemployment and many young people leave school without qualifications.

Kessaci wrote a book, became an activist for the Green party and tried to influence government policy explaining how poor teenagers were easy prey. He described how, aged 10 and in his pyjamas, he sat in the back of his mother’s car as she desperately drove round estates at night trying to pull his brother away from gangs, and was threatened by a gun herself.

But at the height of Kessaci’s public campaigning, in November 2025, another brother – Mehdi, 20, who wanted to join the police force and had no connection to drugs – was shot dead during the day in Marseille. There were street marches and outrage that drug gangs were using violence to try to threaten anyone who spoke out and the state appeared powerless.

“The real challenge is to deconstruct the myths around drug dealing,” said Kessaci, who this year was elected as a deputy mayor of Marseille. “We’re seeing in all these different TV series turning drug barons into heroes … They’re telling children Pablo Escobar [the notorious Colombian cartel boss] was someone good, when history does not show that’s true.”

The reality, Kessaci said, was that on housing estates in Marseille and elsewhere in France people were forced to live with dealers running checkpoints, young boys being recruited instead of attending school and drug gangs filling “a void” left by a lack of public services.

“Young people [in France] are being sold an illusion [by these gangs] that they can make €500 a day … But young people are the first to be killed in these drug wars. And at the summit you have a handful of people living very well off it.”

Kessaci said the French state had to go after French drug kingpins living abroad, in Dubai or elsewhere. Young boys were being recruited through a “capitalist lie” about making money in drugs, when in fact young dealers were left destitute and exposed to dehumanising violence, he added.

“It’s an enormous challenge today, in particular in Marseille, to fight against this idea of ‘Kalashnikov cool’. It’s a civilisational challenge … We’re in a war of civilisation – that’s a term used by the far right, but I refuse to leave that term to them. We have to reappropriate it because we’re in a war to show children that human life is worth more than money.”

For teenagers on an estate who see their parents getting into debt to pay bills and who feel abandoned by the school system, “they are looking to belong to a community”, Kessaci said, and they fall for what he called the drug gangs’ “smoke and mirrors” promise of high earnings.

For Kessaci, the solution is social and economic: better public services and education. “You can break the myth of narco gangs if schools allow children to dream again, to have a perspective for the future … I get really angry with influencers who show a life that’s not true – filming in Dubai with cars, apartments, restaurants, clubs, an astronomical spend on wine. It’s all fake.”

The 23-year-old currently heads Marseille’s social housing organisation and wants to tackle the impact of housing on children falling into drug crime. He has support across the city as many other bereaved families work to try to keep teenagers from crime.

“It’s not possible for this to continue, so I’m trying to give children and teenagers another horizon,” said Farida Chater, who runs a youth and sports association on the Visitation housing estate in Marseille. Her aim is to keep teenagers occupied and away from drug recruiters.

“I’ve suffered myself, I lost my son-in-law in a shooting in 2019,” Chater said. “Now I want to protect the next generation, to show there are better options, to not be tempted by false promises of easy money.”

articles.title: Cuts force World Food Programme to end support for half a million Palestinians in Gaza
articles.summary: Two-thirds of population face crisis levels of food insecurity and 200,000 people are in danger of famine
body: This winter is likely to deepen hunger for Palestinians in Gaza, after sweeping aid cuts forced the UN’s World Food Programme (WFP) to end support for more than half a million people each month, the agency’s director for Palestine said.
More than a year after a Trump-brokered ceasefire came into force, promised reconstruction has not begun, there are few jobs and the vast majority in Gaza still rely on aid to eat.
This summer, WFP programmes helped feed three-quarters of Gaza’s population, about 1.6 million people, but funding has fallen by more than half from 2025 levels.

As a result, from October, aid has been scaled back to 1.1 million people each month. Cuts to deliveries of ration boxes, cash stipends to buy food in markets, and hot meals at community kitchens have already been rolled out.
The WFP needs more than £300m over the next six months to restore and maintain critical programmes in Palestine.
A year of large aid shipments ended a famine declared in summer 2025 and reduced the most severe hunger, but without steps to rebuild Gaza’s economy, most families still rely on food handouts.
“These are very fragile gains, easily reversed, and the situation is still brutal,” said Shaun Hughes, the WFP’s representative and country director for Palestine.

Two-thirds of the population in Gaza face crisis levels of food insecurity, phase three under the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC), which is used to assess if a population is approaching famine.

Food insecurity is at emergency levels for 200,000 Palestinians, which means immediate humanitarian supplies are needed to prevent deaths from hunger, Hughes said. This is IPC phase four, one step away from famine conditions.

Young children and their mothers are particularly vulnerable. After enduring years of food shortages, one in eight children in Gaza are chronically malnourished or stunted, a recent Unicef survey found, and may have suffered permanent damage.
Most humanitarian organisations are struggling with funding after the Trump administration decimated USAID and other donor nations cut aid spending as they grapple with cost of living crises.

The famine and war brought global attention to Gaza last year, ensuring funding. With a nominal ceasefire in place and the most extreme malnutrition curbed, the crisis there has slipped out of headlines and fatigue has set in among many donors.

However aid will be needed at scale until Israel and the international community launch the large-scale reconstruction promised last year. There is no way for most people to feed their own families at present, because about 80% of Gaza’s population is unemployed, according to UN data.

“We need to invest in recovery. This humanitarian operation isn’t affordable or sustainable in the long term,” Hughes said. “Ultimately that’s also what everyone in Gaza is telling us. They really don’t want to be reliant on these handouts, don’t want to stand in the hot meals queue every day. They want to have some chance of stability and recovery.”

Gaza was self-sufficient in fruit and vegetables before the war, but the vast majority of farmland has been occupied by Israel’s military. The sophisticated greenhouse and irrigation systems that supported agricultural production have been destroyed.
Fish has historically been a key source of protein in the territory, but the Israeli navy bars fishing boats from waters off the coast.
Alaa Sarhan, 40, lives with his wife and five children aged between four and 16 in a tent near the “yellow line” the marker of Israeli control. They have already noticed the impact of the WFP cuts.

“In recent days, we have had to plan our meals around what is available rather than what we want to eat,” he said. A former paramedic, he was injured by Israeli attacks nearly two decades ago, and his disability benefits buy very little.
“Often, I give up my share of food so my children can eat. I got accustomed to doing this because the most important thing is that they have something to eat.”

For three years, Israeli restrictions on aid shipments have been the main driver of hunger and malnutrition in Gaza. For months at a time, entry of food was restricted or entirely barred as Palestinians went hungry inside the territory.

Now, for the first time since October 2023, lack of funds may also become an obstacle to feeding hungry Palestinians. Israel’s controls on shipments into Gaza exacerbate funding shortfalls, because they make humanitarian work particularly expensive compared with other parts of the world.

Limits on fuel, engine oil and spare parts, and complex, opaque shipping restrictions push up transport time and costs. Mass destruction of buildings by airstrikes means warehouse space is limited and costly.

Even an influx of cash might not allow the WFP to immediately reverse the cuts. Sourcing and shipping the ingredients for ration boxes can take about three months, and the reduction of cash transfers may already be affecting supply chains.

The injection of more than £30m a month has “underpinned purchasing power for the private sector in Gaza”, Hughes said, allowing trucks to come in with relatively expensive shipments of both healthy and unhealthy food.
For now, the WFP has tried to reduce the impact of funding cuts by scaling back these programmes rather than cutting them entirely. Families who get ration boxes will receive one, rather than two.

But even limited reductions may push families with no other food source or income back into dangerous levels of malnutrition. For the poorest of the poor, reduced rations don’t work, Hughes said. “There’s only so far you can cut [support] until you don’t have the food security impact at the household level.”

The WFP is trying to monitor hunger levels so they reach the most vulnerable, monitoring “negative coping strategies”. These include whether people have skipped meals, or are seeking exploitative and dangerous work.

Nesreen Muqayed, 50, lives with her husband, four children and two grandchildren. She needs a regular diet to manage kidney problems, and a grandson who is on the autism spectrum cannot tolerate many foods.

Despite these urgent medical needs, they often go hungry. “Sometimes we try to save part of a meal for breakfast because we do not know whether we will have anything to eat the following day,” Muqayed said. “The situation has become more difficult over the past two weeks.”
The hot meals from community kitchens that make up a large part of their diet have only been delivered every other day in October, and their meagre backup supplies are already running out.

“I used the last of our flour yesterday,” she said. Beyond grappling with daily hunger, she also finds it painful denying her children healthy food they want and need for their development, because they cannot even afford bananas.

“Sometimes I pass a fruit seller and look at what he has on display, but I do not have the money to buy,” she said. “Fruit and vegetables have become luxuries that we cannot afford regularly, even though they are basic necessities that every family should be able to access.”

articles.title: Three deaths from float crushes raise safety concerns over Japanese festivals
articles.summary: Deputy mayor of Saijo died after becoming trapped under float, days after two similar incidents elsewhere
body: There is mounting concern over the safety of Japan’s traditional festivals after the death of a senior local official who was reportedly crushed beneath a float at the weekend, days after two men died in similar incidents in another part of the country.
