Akihiro Nabae, the deputy mayor of Saijo, in western Japan, was carrying a giant float with other participants in a festival on Saturday when he became trapped beneath the structure, Agence France-Presse reported. Nabae, 62, was taken to hospital and later pronounced dead, local media said, adding that no one else was injured.

He died less than two weeks after a 51-year-old man was crushed beneath a wooden float he was riding at one of the annual Danjiri festivals held in southern Osaka prefecture. The same day, a 48-year-old man was killed in a similar accident at a Danjiri event in a nearby town. Police said 16 people were injured in the incidents.

The accidents occurred when the floats, which can weigh up to 4 tonnes, toppled as they were being pulled at speed around tight corners by hundreds of men, police said. The turns, known as yarimawashi, are a highlight of the festivals, originally held to pray for good autumn harvests.
It is not clear if Nabae lost his balance or if the contraption toppled on to him, according to police in Saijo, where the festival has been held annually since the Edo period (1603-1868).
Media reports said 11 floats, each weighing as much as 3 tonnes, were lined up side by side at the time of the accident.
The annual Saijo festivals, featuring more than 100 floats, are held to thank Shinto deities for plentiful grain crops, the Jiji news agency said.

Saijo’s mayor, Mitsuyoshi Ochi, voiced shock and sadness at Nabae’s death. “Just when we were about to work together to build a new administration for Saijo, this tragedy occurred. I still can’t believe it. I offer my heartfelt condolences,” he said in a statement.

In February, two people died in a crush at the “naked man festival” in Okayama, where as many as 10,000 men dressed in fundoshi loincloths squeeze into the grounds of a temple and compete to seize a pair of sacred wooden sticks thrown into the crowd by the head priest. The two men who succeed are declared “lucky men” for the year.

articles.title: US gave us no warning of Russian strikes on Kyiv power plants, Zelenskyy says
articles.summary: Ukrainian president accuses Washington of ‘denial of reality’ in continuing row with Trump over apparent support for Moscow
body: Ukraine did not receive a warning from the US about an impending Russian missile attack on Sunday evening, Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said, reviving concerns that Washington is withholding intelligence to bully Kyiv into capitulating to Moscow.

Yuri Ihnat, a spokesperson for the Ukrainian air force, said on television on Monday morning that Ukraine had not received a warning before a Russian missile barrage hit power plants in Kyiv at about 11pm. Earlier, a Ukrainian government official had told the Guardian the US had not warned the capital about the impending missile strike.
Ukraine did receive a warning before a subsequent strike, at 3am, Ihnat added.

“Once again, Russia launched a ballistic missile attack in multiple waves throughout the night, and once again, there was no warning from our partners,” Zelenskyy wrote in a social media post on Monday morning.

“When the supply of missiles for Ukrainian air defence is blocked, and Russia receives sanctions relief or delays, it is, unfortunately, a denial of reality on the part of our partners,” the president added.
Zelenskyy is grappling with recent US moves benefiting the Russian president, Vladimir Putin.

On Friday, Donald Trump waived a sweeping package of sanctions on Russia, telling Congress the pause on the legislation, named after the late senator Lindsey Graham and passed by both chambers, was in the national interest. Ukraine has also complained of slowed deliveries of PAC-3 air defence missiles from the US.

The US president wrote on Truth Social on Sunday: “My decision on Russia is a very simple one. I am in the process of negotiating peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine, and don’t want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table.
“Zelenskyy doesn’t care, and frankly, with all of the money that Europe is famously giving him … he doesn’t want to end this war, and probably never did.”

Trump also told reporters on Monday that he would consider a trilateral meeting with Russia and China. He said: “We ‌would have it to talk about nuclear weapons and denuclearisation. If ‌President Xi wants to have it, I’d ​have it.”

For years, the US has warned Ukraine before Russia launched ballistic missiles, giving authorities several minutes to sound alarms and allow civilians to reach shelters before the strikes hit. However, Ukraine has said it was not warned on at least three days in the past week before missiles were launched, amid a public quarrel between Zelenskyy and Trump.

Speaking in the early hours of Monday on a trip to Samarkand, Uzbekistan, the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said: “If it happened last night, I don’t know exactly. I know a few nights ago there was a software problem involving their early warning system.”

US officials have not previously mentioned a software glitch in the early warning system. In at least one case, Ukrainian officials had been told that bad weather over southern Russia had obscured preparations for the missile launch. Rubio said the military’s European Command was looking into the strikes.

The US has maintained plausible deniability as services and programmes provided to support Ukraine have suddenly begun to fail. The Trump administration has denied that it throttled services in Ukraine for Starlink, the satellite internet service run by Elon Musk that is used both on offensive drones and anti-air weapons by Ukraine.

Ukraine has also said US weapons delivered through the PURL scheme, where Europe purchases US weapons then delivers them to Ukraine, have been delayed. The Trump administration reportedly threatened Kyiv with a slowdown in crucial weapons deliveries unless it stopped striking Russian oil refineries.
On Sunday, Ukraine launched more than 1,000 drones at Russia in one of its largest aerial attacks of the war, setting fire to an oil export terminal and a depot in St Petersburg.

The Russian barrage on Sunday evening hit 28 substations and other critical energy facilities, depriving more than 500,000 people of electricity, heat and running water, Zelenskyy said on social media. Russia has sought to disrupt daily life in Ukraine by attacking trains, shopping centres, fuel stations and supermarkets, among other sites.
Russia fired 16 ballistic missiles at Kyiv and the surrounding region, Zelenskyy said, and officials in the capital reported that a 21-year-old woman had been killed.

Later drone strikes on a public park in the north-eastern Kharkiv region killed six people, including young children. The regional governor, Oleg Synegubov, said on Telegram that three of the dead in the attack on Nova Vodolaha were children, including one in a pushchair. Seven children were among the 14 wounded. Police posted pictures showing damaged playground equipment.

Synegubov condemned “another terrorist act by the Russian Federation”, saying “the enemy strikes a recreational park in the middle of the day, knowing that there is no military infrastructure there at all”.

Pope Leo XIV spoke by phone with Zelenskyy on Monday to discuss the embattled city of Oleshky in Ukraine’s Kherson region, according to a Vatican statement. He told the Ukrainian president that he had asked Putin for a humanitarian ceasefire during a call with the Russian leader on Friday.

Residents of Oleshky face a worsening humanitarian crisis, with shortages of food and medication, as they are caught in the crossfire between Russian and Ukrainian troops. The Vatican said that Leo had expressed deep concern about conditions in the city and sought a ceasefire to permit aid deliveries and evacuations.
The call to Zelenskyy came two days after Leo, 71, was discharged from a hospital in Rome where he underwent a lung cancer operation on Tuesday.
The Kremlin said on Friday it had explained to Leo what it called “the Kyiv regime’s responsibility for the difficult humanitarian situation”.

articles.title: Monday briefing: What you need to know about a weekend of chaos in France
articles.summary: In today’s newsletter: Violent riots and looting have dominated the headlines, but the unrest gripping the country and beyond reflects deeper public anger over everyday issues
body: Good morning. I bet your weekend was better than Emmanuel Macron’s. On Friday, the evening before mass protests that were planned across France, he attended a Céline Dion concert in Paris with his wife, Brigitte, prompting comparisons to Louis XVI and Marie Antoinette. On Sunday evening, he was forced to give a televised speech condemning the “unbridled violence” and riots that erupted in French cities over the weekend.

The rioters that burned makeshift barricades of bicycles in Paris, destroyed the steeple of Limoges’ town hall and set fire to Lyon’s tourism office were described as “LE CHAOS” on the front page of La Tribune Dimanche, and “SCENES D’INSURRECTION” on Le Parisien Dimanche. By Sunday, protests had also taken place in Spain, Portugal and Italy.
Today’s newsletter explains what happened in France over the weekend, and why this crisis threatens to engulf Macron’s government. First, here are the weekend’s headlines.

The Vatican | Pope Leo told a crowd gathered in St Peter’s Square on Sunday that he would “gradually resume” his activities, at his first appearance before the faithful since undergoing an operation to remove a cancerous tumour from his lung.
UK news | A “well-known individual” is trying to secure a permanent injunction against the Guardian and ITN to prevent them from publishing details of serious allegations made against him.

US politics | Donald Trump fired his immediately embattled new press secretary, Katie Zacharia, on Friday evening after just five days in the job. The conservative commentator becomes the shortest serving occupant of the role in US history.

Reform | A Reform UK mayor is under police investigation for allegedly showing “naked and sexualised” images of himself to a female member of staff. Luke Campbell, a former Olympic boxing champion, is understood to have been questioned under caution by Humberside police.
Energy | The development of a huge AI datacentre hailed by the UK government has received a fresh setback after Microsoft pulled out of the project over concerns about power supplies.

In the early hours of Sunday, cleaners started to remove the detritus from Parisian streets: shards of glass from broken shop windows, smashed bus shelters, burned out cars. The smell of teargas still lingered in the Métro station at Place de la République. “Areas of Paris looked like a wasteland,” Paolo Stuppia, a sociologist at Sciences Po in Paris, tells me. About 855 people have been arrested in Paris, and a total of 2,400 have been arrested across France. Lamia El Aaraje, the Socialist deputy mayor of Paris, said the capital had experienced a level of violence “we had never seen before.”

There have been so many incredible images of destruction (see our gallery here) that it’s possible to forget Saturday was, for the most part, defined by peaceful protests. Hundreds of thousands of people, many of them schoolchildren and parents, joined marches across the country. A far smaller group of protesters, many wearing face masks, smashed street furniture and torched cars and bus stops. A third group took the opportunity to loot shops. “I saw teenagers running off with shoeboxes, clothes, and perfume,” Angelique Chrisafis, the Guardian’s Paris correspondent, tells me.

It’s the second group that has dominated the headlines. On Saturday afternoon, people set the town hall in Limoges alight (its spire collapsed dramatically on Saturday evening), and broke into the city hall in Marseille. “It wasn’t as if the peaceful protesters suddenly turned violent,” Chrisafis says. “It was as if the government didn’t have a hold on the situation, and suddenly, the police were really caught off guard.”
The peaceful protesters ‘Our future is being stolen from us’

When a small number of people break the law during otherwise peaceful protests, there’s a tendency to condemn such acts as “criminality, pure and simple” (to quote David Cameron during the 2011 London riots), and to disqualify the idea they represent a form of antagonism against authority. “If everything was going well in France, you wouldn’t have young kids ransacking stores,” Stuppia says.

Such criminal acts can also become a means of undermining peaceful protesters. “Some of those people are now pretty upset because they believe the government will be talking about burning barricades rather than the fact they turned out in such large numbers,” Chrisafis says. French students have been protesting against the school system since September and calling for repairs to decrepit buildings, smaller class sizes, and reforms to a widely loathed university admissions system. Education is a particularly fraught subject in France, where academic credentials overwhelmingly determine job prospects. But their concerns are also broader; as Greta Thunberg put it recently, “our future is being stolen from us,” a feeling that many young people across the continent share.

The student protests have since become the focus in a constellation of different issues, ranging from the cost of living to rising fuel prices and public service cuts. Those on Saturday drew in numerous groups, including unions and supporters of the Gilets Jaunes. “Gen-Z is really facing a polycrisis of different issues, from the climate crisis to the rise of the far right and the use of AI” Stuppia tells me. “And you can see the same set of issues coming alive in Italy, in Belgium, in Portugal, and with the Cockroach protests in India. Young people want change.” (You can read more about how these protests have spread to other European countries in this story by Sam Jones).
The police ‘Entire cities … left to the mercy of rioters’

The police response has been at once strikingly brutal and remarkably inept. As Guardian columnist Rokhaya Diallo pointed out in this recent opinion piece, French schoolchildren have been “treated like enemies to be crushed” over the last few weeks. French lawyers have said that several teenagers have suffered “war-like” injuries from police, including a 14-year-old boy who suffered a fractured jaw and a 15-year-old whose hand was blown off in an explosion involving a police stun grenade. The number of arrests has also been disproportionate: according to this graph by Pierre Bataille, a sociologist at Grenoble Alpes university, more people were arrested during two weeks of the student protests than members of the Gilets Jaunes were in an entire year.

The shortcomings of this zealous focus on student protesters became clear on Saturday afternoon. Crowd psychologists have demonstrated that rather than instilling order, heavy-handed policing can actually trigger violence. While the police blocked a demonstration route between Place de la République and Place de la Concorde on Saturday citing “serious risks of public disorder,” large sections of Paris were left without enough officers to prevent looting. According to the French Green leader Marine Tondelier, “entire cities were left to the mercy of rioters, while peaceful protesters were subjected to violence.” She has since been calling for the resignation of Laurent Nuñez, France’s minister of the interior, calling his performance over the weekend “an absolute disaster”.
The politicians ‘Social unrest is shaking our country’

In his statement last night, Macron drew a distinction between protesters with “legitimate demands” and “those who destroyed, smashed, and looted”, and criticised “factious groups from the ultra-left, joined by numerous delinquents” (pending an investigation, though, it’s impossible to say what the rioters’ motivations were). There are tricky and enduring questions that his government now faces. It failed to anticipate both the student protests that have engulfed France since September, and the violence that broke out over the weekend. As this interesting New Yorker piece (£) points out Macron’s experience of the public education system is limited, and even his education minister has admitted that at least some of his five children attend private schools.

The protests and the police response have underscored how out of touch Macron’s government appears to be with French people, many of whom are angry about the price of fuel and the cost of living. This sense of disaster – described by the mayor of Limoges, Guillaume Guérin, a member of the conservative Les Républicains party, as a “colossal failure of the state” – has overshadowed the thousands of people who turned out for peaceful protests, and plays into the hands of the far right (Marine Le Pen, who gave her own address on X before Macron’s, has described the riots as a “threat to democracy”). In a recent interview with Le Monde, the mayor of Lyon, Grégory Doucet, struck a more dispassionate tone, and said there need to be “concrete, political answers” to “the social unrest shaking our country.”

articles.title: ‘This is not poker’: Alberta goes to polls in referendum that has exposed divisions, not least among separatists
articles.summary: Voters to be asked whether province should remain part of Canada or hold a second, binding independence vote
body: Albertans are going to the polls to decide their place in Canada, in a referendum that has exposed deep divisions within the province, not least in the separatist movement itself.
On Monday, voters will respond to the question of whether Alberta should remain in Canada, or hold a second, binding independence referendum.

A minority have long argued that separation is the only way to address their belief that Alberta is short-changed by its financial relationship with Ottawa, and prevented from fully exploiting the province’s vast fossil fuel reserves.

Any enthusiasm either side might have held headed into the referendum was muted after a deadly fire broke out at a major military base in the province. On Saturday afternoon, a blaze tore through the CFB Wainwright and into the nearby town. Canada’s armed forces announced with “profound sadness” that there had been multiple deaths and injuries.
The premier of Alberta, Danielle Smith, argued for years that a referendum was not needed, but called one anyway after pressure from some within her United Conservative party.

Nevertheless, Smith did not campaign in favour of independence, saying in June she estimated the cost of separating at about C$400bn (£212bn) for the transition and another $25bn-$50bn in annual costs associated with starting a new country. Smith’s caution prompted some of her supporters to accuse her of betraying the independence movement.

Opponents of independence have focused heavily on the costs of separation, with the University of Calgary’s school of public policy saying in June it could be up to $170bn over a five-year period and be highly unpredictable in the long term.

The issue has not divided neatly along partisan lines. The former premiers Jason Kenney and Rachel Notley – from the rightwing Conservative and leftwing New Democratic party – have appeared on stage together, setting aside a bitter ideological rivalry that more usually defines Albertan politics.
Mark Carney, who grew up in the province, visited both Calgary and Edmonton last week to campaign for a united Canada.

“At this pivotal moment, Albertans have a choice: to build a stronger Alberta and a greater Canada to leave for our children, or to burden them with years of deep division and great uncertainty,” the prime minister told a raucous crowd.
Carney, who previously served as the governor of the Bank of England, saw first-hand the effects of the Brexit vote and the economic upheaval that followed.

“This is not poker. A vote against Canada is a dangerous bluff that will lead to years of deep uncertainty and lost opportunities,” he said. “Our country and your futures are too precious to play games with.”

Carney, whom recent polls identify as the most popular politician in Alberta, joined the former deputy premier of Alberta Thomas Lukaszuk at a rally for the latter’s Forever Canadian group. Lukaszuk has driven more than 40,000km (24,855 miles) around Alberta in a 1992 motorhome named the Unity Bus and distributed at least 100,000 lawn signs.

Rather than campaigning frequently, Carney has pointed to big projects his government is looking to move ahead with that would benefit the province, including a pipeline to the Pacific coast to increase the flow of Alberta crude oil to Asia.
“I won’t sugar-coat it: some of those threads have needed to be repaired. The frustrations that many Albertans have felt are real,” said Carney.

Energy policy has long been at the heart of Alberta’s grievance with Ottawa, stemming from the 1980 national energy programme, which sought greater federal control over the energy sector, provoked fierce opposition in Alberta and helped erode Liberal support across western Canada. The sense that the province’s wealth was being siphoned eastward is older still: a 1915 cartoon, “The Milch Cow”, depicted Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba as farmers feeding a cow whose milk was funnelled into buckets labelled Ottawa, Toronto and Montreal.

“Growing up, I remember. I remember how Ottawa made Albertans feel like our resources weren’t our own,” Carney told the crowd. “And more recently, we were made to feel that our energy contributions were running against the tides of history.”

The movement seeking to capitalise on those grievances, however, has been marked by competing interests, personal rivalries and allegations surrounding some of its leading figures. Jeff Rath, a bombastic lawyer linked to the Alberta Prosperity Project, is alleged to have mismanaged millions of dollars of First Nations trust funds, while David Parker, a longtime rightwing political organiser, was at the centre of a voter-data scandal that exposed the personal information of nearly 3 million Albertans and remains under investigation.

Keith Wilson, one of the principal intellectual and legal architects of the province’s modern separatist movement, recently published the Alberta transition plan, a 214-page blueprint for turning it into an independent country.

Rejecting comparisons to Brexit and the economic fallout, Wilson said: “Every single thing we found that needs to be addressed to do the transition is absolutely doable,” calling most of the tasks “super easy”.
Wilson dismissed the idea that negotiations between an independent Alberta and Canada’s federal government would be acrimonious and lengthy.

“It would be economic suicide for them to challenge Alberta,” he said. “You want to cut off trade with us? OK. By the way, go buy axes and chainsaws because you’re going to have to cut down all the maple trees to keep warm this winter because you’re not going to get our energy products.”

Even within the separatist camp, there are doubts about how quickly independence could be achieved. Bill Jones, a member of the Wildrose Independence party, said its leaders were moving too quickly without the institutions a new country would need, from a police force to a pension system.
“We – Alberta – were always meant to be a colony, to get resources that were here to go east,” said Jones. “And that mindset is still there.”
“I don’t see the evidence for our independence. If we go out today, we’d be a failed state for generations. The great-great-grandchildren would be still suffering. And that’s the problem.”
Monday’s referendum will also include nine other measures unrelated to separation, including proposals affecting social programmes, judicial appointments and the senate.

One remain campaign has distributed thousands of “no to the nine” lawn signs around the province. Even some separatists, angry at Smith, have started a “decline the 9” campaign. Smith, for her part, has pushed a “yes to the rest” message in response.
In Calgary, the city’s mayor said he was “duty bound” to speak out about the perils of an attempt to fracture the country.

“There will be catastrophic impacts that would arise from separation,” said Jeromy Farkas. “And the unfortunate bullshit implication of separation is that it’s invited a conversation about who is a ‘real Canadian’? Who is a ‘real Albertan’? If you are living here in Calgary, you are welcome here. We need to continue to signal that. We need to telegraph that stability.
“We stand to lose so much from simply even having this debate.”

In October, further details emerged about meetings between unelected Alberta separatists and both Republican operatives and staff at the US state department. Among items allegedly discussed were how oil royalties could be directed to the US in exchange for assistance establishing a new country. They also allegedly offered up Alberta’s fresh water resources.

No matter the results on Monday, the referendum could have looked far different if not for the intervention of First Nations, which successfully sued to force the Alberta government to either dismiss the question of separation or change the wording. Key to their argument was the fact that the land of modern-day Alberta is covered by five treaties signed with the crown before the creation of the province.

The president of the Blackfoot Confederacy, Chief Troy “Bossman” Knowlton, said: “These treaties are living documents, but the ignorance of the separatists, and their bigotry, does not allow their mind to accept the fact that they’re not symbolic documents. They have power, and the reality is Alberta does not have the constitutional right to separate.”

Knowlton said that if separatists had proactively reached out to First Nations before pushing ahead with independence, it might have led to a different outcome. “But they treated us as a speed bump they could just drive over.”

He added that the First Nations’ legal victory was followed by what he viewed as recriminations from the province, including an unexplained halt to talks on land claims and cooperation with Alberta’s government.

“At the end of the day, we want Alberta to continue to be a beacon of light,” he said. “Because when the first newcomers came to these lands centuries ago, that’s what our chiefs said: we’ll share these resources we have here. So do we want prosperity for Alberta? You’d better believe it.”

articles.title: Britain cannot deal effectively with geopolitical crises without rejoining EU, says thinktank
articles.summary: ‘Sovereignty without the ability to act on it is not autonomy,’ paper by Institute for Public Policy Research says
body: Britain cannot deal effectively with geopolitical crises such as Russian aggression and political turmoil in the US without rejoining the EU, according to an influential thinktank.

The Institute for Public Policy Research has become the latest organisation close to the Labour party to call for the UK to re-enter the bloc, after Andy Burnham said he wanted to examine all possible options.
The paper, which comes weeks after a similar one from the Tony Blair Institute, adds to growing pressure on the prime minister to back re-entry once his review is over.

Harry Quilter-Pinner, the IPPR’s executive director, said: “The government has made important progress in repairing relations with Europe, but a series of individual deals will not be enough. There is one option which is best for the UK’s relationship with Europe – membership of the EU.
“That does not mean announcing another referendum tomorrow. But this means starting work to move towards this destination, building political support at home and in Europe.”

The IPPR argues that the position taken by the former prime minister Keir Starmer – that the UK should seek closer ties with the EU but not contemplate joining a single market or the bloc as a whole – puts the UK at a disadvantage at a time of global change.

It says Russian expansionism, the lack of reliability from the US as an international partner and increased assertiveness from Beijing mean that the UK should reinforce its power by joining other European nations rather than trying to go it alone.
The paper says: “Sovereignty without the ability to act on it is not autonomy; hedging between larger powers is, at best, a strategy for survival rather than for success.”

It argues that so much has changed since Britain left the EU in 2020 that this would not count as rejoining, but becoming a member of a wholly new European Union. Most voters would be willing to support such a position, it says, citing new polling showing 52% of voters back reentering the union, compared with 29% who oppose such a move.

Voters were likely to be attracted by the promise of shorter queues at passport control in particular, which comes out considerably ahead of economic benefits and the chance to live and work in the EU as potential benefits of membership.

However, they were also likely to be dissuaded by aggressive messaging on migration, with the percentage in favour falling from 52% to 47% once voters are told that rejoining would “open the floodgates” to more migrants. Such a message proved more effective in the polling than one focused on “freedom of movement”, which failed to change the minds of many voters.

The flurry of thinktank reports comes after Burnham signalled he wanted a rethink of Britain’s policy on the EU, announcing at Labour conference he would commission a review of all the options available.
Though the prime minister has not stated his own view as part of that review, he previously told the Guardian he wanted the UK to re-enter the bloc in his lifetime.

Many in government support the idea of rejoining, but worry it could boost support for Nigel Farage and his Reform UK party, which are struggling to overcome controversies over funding and racist views expressed by some party candidates.

articles.title: ‘You reach a tipping point’: New Zealand’s strained healthcare system at centre of election battle
articles.summary: With care shortfalls biting across the country, the National-led coalition has been accused of letting chronic underfunding worsen
body: Back when she was healthy, Jane Harrison worked for the community – securing money for playgrounds, getting kids into sport and making sure her small town in New Zealand’s South Island was ready if an earthquake struck.

Now, she and her husband, Shaun Fitzgerald, 65, are both on disability assistance. Last year, when Fitzgerald – a roofer – was waiting for back surgery for spinal stenosis, Harrison left her job to help look after him at home. The operation in August 2025 was not as effective as hoped. He has since been back into the emergency department in intense pain, waiting for hours with severe cramping, she says. “We called the paramedics recently and they said: ‘There’s no beds in hospital, if we take you you’ll have to sit and you clearly can’t, you’re better off at home.’”

Now, as he waits for another surgery to fuse his vertebrae together, he is hobbling around on a cocktail of daily painkillers, says Harrison, 60. She has long Covid, for which she has struggled to find assistance, and her health has also worsened. “It’s countless trips to the doctor, it’s so expensive, and you have to do it over and over again.”

As New Zealand heads into an election in November, Harrison is among the 44% of the country for whom healthcare is their top concern – second only to the cost of living, according to Ipsos, the political issues monitor. Stretched emergency departments, waiting times of months to see a family doctor, delayed cancer treatments and hard-to-access specialist care are common experiences for people across the country. Critics say chronic underfunding of the health system – exposed during the Covid pandemic – has further cratered under the National-led coalition.
Related: A tight election looms in New Zealand. This time, overseas voters could be bad news for the big parties

For Harrison, her household’s inability to access timely healthcare feels unfair. “Shaun was the biggest, strongest man – he was the guy who would pick up your fridge and put it on the trailer,” she says. “We were energetic people, we’ve worked all our lives, we’ve paid tax. We never imagined we would be in this situation.
“We should not be bed-bound and desperately trying to eke out money from the government.”

The state of healthcare in New Zealand has been thrown into the spotlight in recent months, with high-profile incidents including a man’s death after collapsing in hospital toilets after a nine-hour wait at a busy emergency department at one of the country’s biggest hospitals. A shortage of healthcare professionals is felt across the sector.

“There’s not enough beds, not enough nurses, not enough doctors at every level of the roster, not enough space,” says Dr Katie Ben, an anaesthetist and president of the Association of Salaried Medical Specialists, a doctors’ union.
Related: ‘The future scares me’: why unemployment has become biggest election issue for young New Zealand voters

“It’s been a gradual decline but we’re trying to do more with less and less and you just reach a tipping point.” There are now 17 fewer nurses in Nelson, where she works, than three years ago; surgical wards were run from an earthquake-prone building, earmarked for replacement at least a decade ago, she says.
Nurses and doctors spoken to by the Guardian say their ability to provide safe care is being compromised, and that many are defecting to Australia, where they say the pay could be up to 30% higher.

Combined with the rollback of Māori-access initiatives, millions dished out to private hospitals, and an aging population with higher health demands, Ben says a two-tier healthcare system is emerging where only those who can afford it can be seen. With one in four adults saying they can’t access their GP, record numbers of patients are presenting to emergency departments.

In late August, criticism of the National-led coalition’s approach to health ramped up when it was revealed only 54 additional full-time nurses had been hired since the government came into power, not the 2,000 promised by health minister Simeon Brown.

Brown says the health system is “measurably improving”. Three-quarters of emergency department patients are seen within the target of six hours, and childhood immunisation rates and elective surgery waiting times have improved, he says in a statement. Spending more on private hospitals means 40,000 extra elective surgeries, he says. Brown concedes “the system remains under pressure, and too many New Zealanders are still waiting too long for care”.

In comparison to healthcare in other countries in the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, data shows New Zealand hovers close to the middle; its health expenditure per capita and the number of practising nurses are above average, but the number of hospital beds and doctors are below average.

The latest 1News Verian poll has the National and Labour parties tied on 28%, with the left-leaning Greens at 15%. National’s current coalition partners ACT and NZ First are both polling at 10%, while the centrist Opportunity party is on 8%, and could potentially hold the balance of power in a new government formed under New Zealand’s mixed member proportional system.

If re-elected, National has promised to boost the country’s medicines budget by $604m, by cutting foreign aid outside the Pacific. Labour has said it would reinstate a smoke-free policy and free prescriptions, introduce three free GP visits – paid for with a targeted capital gains tax – and guarantee jobs for graduate nurses.
Related: ‘So hacked off’: as election nears, New Zealanders despair at the main parties – and Opportunity knocks

Labour health spokesperson Dr Ayesha Verrall says its priorities are prevention and primary care. “The cost-of-living crisis has made these investments all the more important because people are missing out.”

But for those still waiting months to see their doctor, it’s all still talk. Mother-of-three Abbey Bambry, who lives in the small North Island town of Pahiatua, says residents are often forced to travel 45 minutes to the closest city to see an after-hours doctor, for up to $245 for an adult visit. She has tried writing to the local MP, saying she has seen friends with serious health issues suffer. Seeing pledges to address it properly would sway her vote, she says.
“It concerns me that many people’s only option is to travel for health, and if they do they pay massive fees to get the healthcare they need.
“It’s just like what the hell are we doing, you know?”

articles.title: Four people killed in ‘violent, fast-moving’ fire at Canadian military base
articles.summary: Prime minister Mark Carney describes blaze as ‘one of the worst tragedies for the forces on Canadian soil in peacetime’
body: Four people have been killed and dozens more seriously injured after a “violent, fast-moving” fire tore through one of Canada’s busiest military training bases in Alberta, the country’s prime minister said on Sunday.
Mark Carney called the incident “one of the worst tragedies for the forces on Canadian soil in peacetime”.

Winds up to 96km/h (60mph) fed the blaze, which broke out at 4pm on Saturday during high-intensity combat training at the base. Alberta premier Danielle Smith said at a press conference on Sunday evening that 39 people were in hospital after the fire, with at least 19 of them in a critical condition.

Maj Gen Wade Rutland, commander of the 1st Canadian Division, said that a grass fire ignited in a training area of the military base, which spread quickly. The cause of the fire was being investigated, he said.

The military identified those killed as Sgt Morgan Wong of the Loyal Edmonton Regiment and Privates Shaun Farrell, Aidan Goulding and Hayden Lykkemark of the 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light infantry. All four were serving with the battalion, based in Edmonton.
Rutland said military officials knew about the fire for hours but believed it was contained before winds suddenly shifted, sending flames racing toward the soldiers.
“The fire was a kilometre away when the wind shifted. That is not normal for a fire to move a kilometre in 36 seconds,” he said at a news conference in Edmonton.
“I’ve certainly never seen anything like it,” he added.

The fire broke out during high-intensity combat training involving Charlie Company of the 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light infantry, sweeping into the area where the simulated attacks were taking place.
About 84 soldiers were in the company, which was split between a grenade range and an area where soldiers practised attacks on simulated enemy positions.

“The nation is in mourning for those brave members of our armed forces whom we have lost. And I have asked the flags on all federal buildings to be flown at half-mast to honour them,” Carney told the nation in an address from Ottawa. “We are praying for the wounded.”
Carney said he had requested a “detailed account” from military officials on the ground about what had happened.
The country’s defence minister, David McGuinty, described the event as a “terrible incident” as he travelled to the scene to meet senior officials and first responders.
“I cannot recall an incident like this in recent memory,” he said, adding that the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) were involved in the investigation.

McGuinty did not provide details about what caused the incident and the Canadian armed forces said on Sunday that its “immediate priority” was notifying next of kin and helping those affected by the fire. The armed forces and federal, provincial and local authorities were coordinating the emergency response, they said.
Canada’s top soldier, Gen Jennie Carignan, who serves as chief of the defence staff, called the incident “a profoundly difficult moment for the entire Canadian armed forces”.
The nearby community of Wainwright provided hospital and firefighting support. Flares were spotted in the sky and military medical paratroopers dropped in on a local school football field.
Health staff in ‌Edmonton said a “code orange,” or mass-casualty ​event, was declared to coordinate ​the medical response for patients being transported from Wainwright.
A doctor at a hospital in the city of Edmonton, 180km (112 miles) north-west of Wainwright, told Canada’s national broadcaster that Wainwright’s healthcare facilities had been inundated.

“This number of patients would overwhelm the city of Edmonton,” Dr Warren Thirsk, an emergency department physician at the Royal Alexandra hospital, told CBC News. “It is more patients than any of us want to count right now. It’s a disaster. It’s a one in every 15- to 25-year disaster.”

Officials asked people in Edmonton to avoid the emergency department at the University of Alberta hospital in order to prioritise victims from the military base. Air ambulances were dispatched from Saskatoon and Edmonton.
Related: Just 14% of Albertans want independence from Canada. Can a conference in a Calgary ballroom change that?
The fire at the military base swept into the area where the simulated attacks were taking place, crossing established firebreaks before being contained with help from municipal firefighters.
The Canadian military said there were no indications of terrorism.
On Sunday, the Alberta premier described the fire as “heartbreaking” and said it had affected many military personnel.

“On behalf of the government of Alberta, I extend my deepest condolences to the families who have lost loved ones and wish those who have been injured a full recovery. Our thoughts are also with the military personnel, families and colleagues facing uncertainty and grief during this incredibly difficult time,” Smith said.
The premier said many of the injured would require “weeks and months” of specialised, intensive medical care. She is due to travel to meet senior officials in Edmonton.
The Saskatchewan premier, Scott Moe, said his province was sending assistance to Alberta but did not specify what resources were being deployed.

CFB Wainwright is one of Canada’s busiest military training bases, where soldiers prepare for combat operations. It is home to the Canadian Manoeuvre Training Centre, which conducts realistic battlefield exercises, and the 3rd Canadian Division Training Centre, which provides military training.

“On behalf of the Nato military committee, we extend our deepest condolences to the families and loved ones of those who lost their lives in the tragedy at CFB Wainwright, and our wishes for a full recovery to all the injured,” Adm Giuseppe Cavo Dragone, the chair of the Nato military committee, posted on social media. “Those who fell there served our common security, and the military committee will honour their memory.”
Canada’s Conservative leader, Pierre Poilievre, said he had spoken with Carney and the defence minister to offer support to those affected by the fire.
“Pray for Wainwright, everyone,” Poilievre said in a social media post. He urged people in the area to follow emergency instructions and keep roads clear for first responders.
